conversations.title: Canonical factorization of semantic representations: ontology, grounding, and executable models
conversations.coverage_note: Curated excerpts from the visible conversation on 2026-10-18. This is an inquiry map, not a native ChatGPT export or a complete transcript. Excerpts preserve selected questions, hypotheses, distinctions, and the requested next action; intervening wording is omitted. All semantic annotations are proposed and require review.

messages.text: What is a taxonomy? And how does it relate to an ontology? Concisely, and if there isn't a clear meaning then tell me.
A taxonomy organizes categories; an ontology models concepts and how they relate.
I guess I feel like semantic spectrum is a little underspecified and maybe it's something more like a canonical factorization?
A spectrum orders representations, whereas a factorization explains their constituent dimensions.
There must be someone who has already figured this out.
The ontology spectrum is a close match, but I haven't found evidence of one universally accepted, canonical factorization of semantic representation.
Can you make all these terms like grounding, logical constraints, etc. concrete with an example?
Grounding connects identifiers in the representation to what they are intended to refer to; model-theoretic interpretation alone does not establish a real-world correspondence.

With taxonomy it is kind of a claim that is-a is a special or privileged relation type. Why is that, and are there others? Is grounding a model-theory thing? Also, are we missing cardinality, properties, or types?
These are not all merely logical constraints: types, attributes, cardinality, identity, constraints, inference, time, uncertainty, and provenance play different roles.

I feel like the dimensions are arbitrary. Could category theory or database theory help formalize ontology engineering as a canonical factorization? I also imagine an executable or operational ontology: physics has entities, relations, laws, initial conditions, and a runnable model; mathematics and logic have calculations, theorems, and proofs.
A cellular automaton can be described with entities, states, structure, and transition rules; operational semantics and transition systems formalize how descriptions govern execution.
I think there are two approaches: a ground-up formal proof, and checking candidate factorizations against possible representations to make sure the account is MECE. Perhaps they should alternate.

For physics, I imagine a representation of what exists, expanded to include relations and laws, then initial conditions, then a runnable representation. Mathematics and logic have calculations, theorems, and proofs. These may be different forms of representation, some of which can be run, computed, or simulated.
Check out my Inquiry Graph repo, fill out the Inquiry Graph for this conversation, and then let's look for someone who has already worked this out. I don't want to reinvent it.
